name: Amsterdam
info: Amsterdam is a city on the Amstel river in North Holland, first recorded in 1275 as a settlement by a dam, which became a major trading port of the 17th century and is now the capital of the Netherlands.

facts.founded: The settlement grew at the mouth of the Amstel after the flood of 1170, and a dam there is estimated to date from between 1264 and 1275. It is first named in a document of 27 October 1275, which gave its residents an exemption from tolls.
facts.where: At the mouth of the Amstel river, where it meets the IJ, in the province of North Holland in the western Netherlands, about 2 metres below sea level.
facts.known: The dam in the Amstel and the toll privilege of 1275; herring and the Baltic grain trade; the Dutch Golden Age of the 17th century; the Dutch East India Company and its stock exchange; the canal ring; religious refuge for Jews, Huguenots and others; Rembrandt; the occupation of 1940 to 1945 and the deportation of its Jews
facts.today: Amsterdam is the capital and largest city of the Netherlands, though the government and parliament sit in The Hague.

t: Amsterdam grew from a settlement at a dam on the Amstel, first named in 1275, into a trading town of the County of Holland that lived from beer, herring, and grain and timber from the Baltic.

In the 17th century, after the Dutch Revolt and the fall of Antwerp, it became the leading port and financial centre of the western world, with the Dutch East India Company, a bank and a stock exchange, and its canals were built around the old town.

The city declined in the 18th and early 19th centuries, revived with the North Sea Canal and industry, and in the Second World War lost most of its Jewish population, who had made up about a tenth of its people.
dyk: In 1452 a fire destroyed three quarters of Amsterdam, and Emperor Charles decreed that new houses were to be built of stone; the Wooden House in the Begijnhof is one of the few wooden buildings left from this period.
ev: The All Saints' Flood turns the IJ into a wide estuary and gives the Amstel an open connection to the Zuiderzee
Count Floris V grants the residents of Amestelledamme an exemption from tolls
Amsterdam changes sides in the Alteratie and joins the revolt against Spain
The Dutch East India Company is founded, with its Amsterdam office trading in its own shares
The plague kills more than a tenth of the population, with 24,148 buried in that year
The Netherlands is conquered by France and the old Republic becomes the Batavian Republic
The North Sea Canal opens and gives the port a direct route to the sea
Nazi Germany invades the Netherlands and occupies Amsterdam until 1945

sections.origins:
Amsterdam stands at the mouth of the Amstel river in the western Netherlands, in the province of North Holland. Excavations for the North/South metro line found objects of the Neolithic and Roman eras in the old bed of the Amstel under the Damrak and Rokin, among them shards of Bell Beaker pottery dated 2200 to 2000 BCE. The finds point to a modest semi-permanent or seasonal settlement, since the river mouth and banks were too wet for permanent habitation. Farmers lived along the prehistoric IJ and upstream on the Amstel, and in the marshy area called Amestelle land reclamation began as early as the late 10th century.

The Van Amstel family, known in documents by that name since 1019, held the stewardship of this corner of the bishop of Utrecht's district. The All Saints' Flood of 1170 turned the shallow IJ into a wide estuary, which gave the Amstel an open connection to the Zuiderzee. The banks at the river mouth became drier and fit for permanent habitation, and a settlement was built there that looked to traffic, production and trade rather than farming. A dam at the mouth of the Amstel, which gave the Dam its name, is estimated to have been built between 1264 and 1275. The settlement first appears in a document of 27 October 1275, in which Count Floris V of Holland granted its residents a toll exemption.
sections.growth:
Amsterdam's early wealth came from beer, fishing and trade. A toll on Hamburg beer was set in 1323, and the contacts it made led to trade with the Hanseatic cities of the Baltic, from which Amsterdammers increasingly acquired grain and timber in the 14th and 15th centuries. From the 15th century the city ran its own trade route to the Baltic and became the staple market of Europe for bulk cargo, helped by innovations in the herring fishery. Its population was around 1,000 in 1300 and grew through the 15th and 16th centuries, reaching around 50,000 by 1600.

The fall of Antwerp to Spanish forces in 1585 sent many people from the Southern Netherlands north, and between 1585 and 1610 the population more than doubled. How far these migrants made Amsterdam's rise is disputed. In the 17th century the city became the wealthiest in the western world. Its ships sailed to the Baltic, the Caribbean, North America, Africa, Indonesia, India, Sri Lanka and Brazil, and its merchants held the largest share in the Dutch East India Company and the Dutch West India Company. The Bank of Amsterdam began operating in 1609. From the 17th century the city also took part in the Atlantic slave trade as a major destination port for Dutch slave ships in the triangular trade, which lasted until the Netherlands' part in it was abolished in 1814 at the request of the British government. From 1613 the city expanded around its canals, and in the 1660s it reached about 200,000 people. It stayed near 240,000 for most of the 18th century, and its population reached a high of 872,000 in 1959.
sections.rulers:
The Van Amstel family governed the area on behalf of the bishop of Utrecht, while the counts of Holland pressed for power over it. After Floris V was murdered in 1296 Amstelland again belonged to the bishopric. The bishop of Utrecht gave Amsterdam city rights in 1300 or 1306, and after the death of Bishop Gwijde van Henegouwen in 1317 Count Willem III inherited the area, which brought Amsterdam under the County of Holland. In 1342 Count Willem IV granted the city the Groot Privilege.

In the 16th century the city was part of the Habsburg Netherlands, of which Philip II of Spain was lord from 1555. When almost all Dutch cities joined the revolt led by William I of Orange in 1572, Amsterdam stayed loyal to the king, and in 1578 it changed sides in a bloodless revolution called the Alteratie. A closed oligarchy of regents then governed the city, and only men of enough wealth and long enough residence could join it. Prominent regent families included the Boelens Loen, De Graeff, Bicker, Pauw and Hooft.

After the French conquest of 1795 Amsterdam passed through the Batavian Republic and the Kingdom of Holland, and in 1810, when the Netherlands was annexed to the First French Empire, it was declared the third imperial capital after Paris and Rome. Citizens drove out the remaining French on 16 November 1813. In the United Kingdom of the Netherlands (1815 to 1830) it was the capital and largest city, but The Hague and Brussels were the centres of government. Today it is the constitutional capital of the Netherlands, and the government sits in The Hague.
sections.life:
Amsterdam's social make-up changed with each wave of arrivals. Almost a third of the population in the first half of the 17th century were immigrants, most of them Germans, usually Lutheran, with smaller groups of French Huguenots and Sephardic and Ashkenazi Jews. Craftsmen had to join guilds, serve in the city patrol and cooperate in their district, which brought quick integration. Wealthy Sephardic Jews from Portugal were welcomed with all privileges except citizenship, while poor Ashkenazi Jews were vetted more carefully and those who became dependent on the city were encouraged to move on. Armenian merchants, who held a monopoly on Iranian silk, also settled there.

After 1578 Calvinism was the official religion and Catholics could no longer hold mass in public, though clandestine churches in private houses were tolerated, as were Lutheran and Mennonite ones. Only members of the Reformed Church could hold public office. The Jews received permission to practise their religion in 1603, the first synagogue was consecrated in 1639, and the Portuguese Synagogue opened in 1675. The regents spent heavily on waterways, almshouses, hospitals and churches. The city's first theatre opened in 1638, opera could be seen from 1677, and Rembrandt painted in the 17th century. Flemish printers and the city's intellectual tolerance made Amsterdam a centre for the European free press.
sections.crises:
Fire struck the city in 1421 and again in 1452, when three quarters of it was destroyed. In 1534 the authorities, following an imperial decree against the Anabaptists, executed 71 Mennonites in two years and exiled others. When Amsterdam stayed loyal to Spain in 1572, the rebels blocked its port and the city quickly became impoverished. From 1663 to 1666 bubonic plague, supposed to have come from Algiers, struck the city, and in 1664 24,148 people were buried, more than a tenth of the population. During the Napoleonic Wars the Continental System brought severe impoverishment and Amsterdam's significance reached its lowest point.

In the Palingoproer of 1886 the army killed 26 demonstrators. In the First World War food became scarce, and when working-class women began to plunder a ship with army supplies, soldiers opened fire, killing six people and wounding almost 100.

Nazi Germany invaded the Netherlands on 10 May 1940. Around 60,000 Jews lived in Amsterdam, and on 22 February 1941 427 Jewish men were arrested and sent to Mauthausen, from which only two survived. The February strike, in which 300,000 people took part, was a protest against the arrests. Two waves of arrests in 1943 led to deportations, and more than 100,000 Dutch Jews were deported, among them Anne Frank and her sister Margot. During the hunger winter of 1944 an estimated 20,000 people died in Amsterdam and other cities of the west. Allied bombing of the Fokker plants killed more than 200 civilians in Amsterdam-Noord.
sections.legacy:
The canal belt, the Grachtengordel of the Herengracht, Keizersgracht and Prinsengracht, was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in July 2010. The Amsterdam Stock Exchange, founded in 1602 by one account and 1611 by another, is considered the oldest modern securities market in the world. The end of the 19th century is sometimes called the city's second Golden Age: the Concertgebouw was built in 1886 and Centraal Station in 1889, and the Rijksmuseum and the Stedelijk Museum were built by its end. Its ring of 45 forts, the Stelling van Amsterdam, was built to defend it.

The city grew in the 20th century. On 1 January 1921 it annexed neighbouring municipalities, and in 1932 the Afsluitdijk closed the Zuiderzee off from the North Sea, so that Amsterdam no longer had an open connection to the sea. The Amsterdam-Rhine Canal was completed in 1952. After the Second World War the diamond trade, largely in Jewish hands, had essentially disappeared, and few Jews returned. A metro line opened in 1977, and the demolition of the old Jewish quarter led to the Nieuwmarkt riots, after which the planned highway was never fully built.

Amsterdam is today the capital and largest city of the Netherlands, with more than 930,000 inhabitants.

summary: Amsterdam grew from a settlement at a dam on the Amstel, first named in 1275, into the leading port and financial centre of the western world in the 17th century. Declining after 1700, it revived with canals and industry, and is now the capital of the Netherlands.
references: Willem Frijhoff, Geschiedenis van Amsterdam. Zelfbewuste stadsstaat 1650–1813 (SUN, 2005)
Geert Mak, Een kleine geschiedenis van Amsterdam (Atlas, 1994)
Hubert Nusteling, Welvaart en werkgelegenheid in Amsterdam 1540–1860. Een relaas over demografie, economie en sociale politiek van een wereldstad (De Bataafsche Leeuw, 1985)
notes: START: the History article says the first inhabitants settled around 1000 CE; the main article says a settlement was built immediately after the flood of 1170 and the dam dates between 1264 and 1275. I used 1275, the first document, as start, and left the 1000 CE claim out.
CITY RIGHTS: 1300 or 1306 (main article) against 1306 (History). Given as 1300 or 1306 in the text; left out of the events.

STOCK EXCHANGE: the main article says the VOC office became the first stock exchange in 1602; the History article says the exchange was founded in 1611 and the VOC in 1602. Both dates given in legacy; the event says only that the VOC was founded with an office trading in its own shares.
LIBERATION 1945: main article says Canadian forces liberated the city on 5 May 1945; History says Germans surrendered on 5 May, shooting on the Dam on 7 May, and Canadians arrived on 8 May. Left out.
NORTH SEA CANAL: the main article says it opened in 1876; History says approval in 1863. Used 1876.
ANNEXATION OF 1921: the two articles list different municipalities, so I wrote only that neighbouring municipalities were annexed on 1 January 1921.
WWI RIOTS: History gives six killed and almost 100 wounded; main says 'several killed'. Used History.
HUNGER WINTER: the 20,000 deaths are an estimate for Amsterdam and the other cities of the west, as the article says.
The History article's claims about Armenians, the 'Venice of the North' and many canal figures (165 canals, 75 km versus more than 100 km, 90 islands) disagree; left out.
Population 1750 and the 1,000 in 1300 as in the main article. 'More than 930,000' follows History (931,298 in January 2024); the main article gives 941,873 for 2026.

The 1204 attack on the Van Amstel keep, the Miracle of Amsterdam (1345, a legend) and Tulip mania were left out for space. Slave trade involvement (main article) and the Atlantic port role were left out for space; the editor may wish to add them.
Left out as tourism, rankings or the present: tourism figures, sin-city passages, airports, company headquarters, the 2024 museum opening.
